source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive Capabilities of LLMs: An Exploration in Mathematical Problem Solving
finding: GPT-4 named math skills (about 5000 fine skills on MATH, clustered to 117), then solved test items with exemplars of the named skill. This is metacognitive knowledge used as a retrieval key.
numbers: MATH, GPT-4-0613, text CoT: complex CoT 50.30; topic-based exemplars 50.31; skill-based exemplars 53.88 (about +3.6 points). Skill labels from GPT-3.5 gave 51.9.
limits: Gain is over topic labels that cost the same; one model family; skills were labelled by GPT-4 from training data, so it needs a training set. Not a stuck detector.
agent_relevance: Naming the needed skill before solving is cheap and measured. Fits S1/S2 (represent) more than S6, but a skill label could be the first step of picking an operator at an impasse.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive Capabilities of LLMs
finding: Same skill-exemplar method on GSM8K; random exemplars do not help, skill-matched ones do.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-4-0613: CoT 93.00; CoT + random exemplars 92.87; CoT + skill-based 94.31; skill-based with maj@5 95.38. Code-based MATH variant: +7.52% over baseline (stated in intro).
limits: Near ceiling on GSM8K, so the gain is small in points. Self-consistency stacks on top.
agent_relevance: Matching matters, not just having examples: supports typed retrieval over random few-shot.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: With oracle correctness labels, self-correction looks strong. The oracle tells the model when to stop, which a real agent lacks.
numbers: Oracle table. GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0 (rows paired by order in the extracted table).
quote: the improvements vanish when oracle labels are not available
limits: Table text was extracted from PDF and rows are interleaved; pairing is by row order. Oracle use is the flaw the paper attacks.
agent_relevance: Reflexion-style gains partly come from knowing when the answer is wrong. This is why G2 and G3 need code-located failures, not the model's opinion.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Intrinsic self-correction (no external signal) lowers math accuracy. Rounds of self-correction make it worse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K: 75.9 standard, 75.1 round 1, 74.7 round 2. CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0, 49.0, 43.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time; when it changes, correct-to-wrong is more common than wrong-to-correct.
limits: 2023 models, prompts of the Kim et al. style; later reasoning models behave differently (see c14, c17).
agent_relevance: A scheduled 'are you sure?' step damages correct answers. Direct support for G1 (doubt only on a signal).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Multi-agent debate does not beat self-consistency at equal numbers of responses.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-3.5: 1 response 76.7; self-consistency 3 responses 82.5, 6 responses 85.3, 9 responses 88.2; debate with 6 responses 83.2, 9 responses 83.0 (pairing by extracted table order).
limits: Table layout is garbled in extraction; the headline conclusion is explicit in the paper (section 4 title).
agent_relevance: Supports G9 and abandoning ideas by resampling rather than by argument.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Models find the first wrong step in their own chain of thought poorly, even on objective tasks. Correction works once the location is given.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2186 CoT traces, 5 tasks. GPT-4 best, with overall mistake-finding accuracy 52.87 under direct step-level prompting. GPT-3.5-Turbo as low as 10.10 on one task cell.
limits: PaLM 2 generated traces; accuracy varies by task; a small trained classifier on out-of-domain data beat prompting a large model for location.
agent_relevance: Monitoring failure is the bottleneck, not repair. S5 should get the failing step from code; S6 should not trust a model's 'I am stuck' judgement (matches the r = .17 note in SCHEMA).

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Feeding the true mistake location boosts downstream accuracy on all 5 tasks; a cheap trained classifier can supply a location without ground truth.
numbers: Improvement on 5 of 5 reasoning tasks reported with gold location; exact per-task deltas not copied here.
limits: Gold location is an upper bound. The classifier is out-of-domain and imperfect.
agent_relevance: A step-level locator (code, PRM or small classifier) is worth more than a bigger self-critic. Fits G2.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey
finding: Critical survey of self-correction papers. No prior work shows success from feedback of a prompted LLM, except tasks specially suited to it.
numbers: Three findings: (1) no successful self-correction from prompted-LLM feedback outside very suitable tasks; (2) works where reliable external feedback exists; (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it. The bottleneck is feedback generation.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Survey, not new experiments; covers work to 2024.
agent_relevance: Agrees with G2/G3. S6 triggers must be external signals (failed checks, repeated errors), not self-assessed confidence.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflexion fires its self-reflection on a hand-written stuck rule, then stores a verbal lesson. A direct computational twin of Schoenfeld-style control.
numbers: ALFWorld, 134 tasks: trigger is same action and same response for more than 3 cycles, or more than 30 actions. ReAct + Reflexion completed 130 of 134 tasks over 12 trials; ReAct alone stalled between trials 6 and 7 and kept a 22% hallucination rate.
quote: if the agent executes the same action and receives the same response for more than 3 cycles
limits: GPT-3-era models; the rule needs environment feedback; a separate LLM-classifier variant was also tried alongside the heuristic.
agent_relevance: A concrete, code-side S6 trigger: repeated identical action-result pairs, or a step cap. Cheap and measured.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Reflexion also gains on reasoning and code where there is a real test signal.
numbers: Abstract: HumanEval pass@1 91%. Intro: gains over strong baselines of 22% (AlfWorld), 20% (HotPotQA), 11% (HumanEval) absolute.
limits: Huang et al. argue part of the QA gain rests on oracle labels (c03). Code tests are real signals; QA labels may not be.
agent_relevance: Reflect only where code can say pass or fail. Matches G2.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models abandon approaches too early. Wrong answers contain far more thought switches. This is Schoenfeld's wild-goose-chase failure seen in models: many half-tried approaches, no depth.
numbers: On average o1-like models used 225% more tokens in incorrect than in correct responses, with 418% more frequent thought-switching. Models: QwQ-32B-Preview, DeepSeek-R1-Preview, R1-671B. Sets: MATH500, GPQA Diamond, AIME2024. Switching rises with difficulty.
quote: frequently switch between different reasoning thoughts without sufficiently exploring promising paths
limits: Switch detection is by marker words (for example 'alternatively'); open-weight models only.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable abandon-too-soon signal: count approach switches. A switch counter could gate S6 against switching before an approach got a fair try.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: In wrong responses, early thoughts are often correct but dropped. The paper defines an underthinking score for how soon a correct thought was left.
numbers: Figure 5 and text: a notable share of the first thoughts in incorrect responses were correct but not pursued; the weighted UT score is reported per model and set. Exact per-index percentages are in the figure and not reliably readable from the text.
limits: Figure numbers garbled in extraction; the qualitative claim is explicit.
agent_relevance: Supports S4 harvesting: keep abandoned candidates and test them (SCHEMA S4 already does).

source: Wang et al. (2025) Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Thought Switching Penalty (TIP) lowers the logit of switch tokens for a window after each thought starts. It raised accuracy with no fine-tuning.
numbers: Pass@1 (32 samples): AIME2024 QwQ-32B-Preview 38.3 to 44.1; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 61.4 to 64.1; DeepSeek-R1 73.8 to 74.8 (a prompt-only version gave 72.4). On AIME2024 R1 switch tokens fell 13.8 to 5.7 and the interval between them rose 580.1 to 941.6 tokens.
limits: Gains are about 1 to 6 points; needs logit access; the prompt-only version did not help.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to stay on it by prompt fails; a mechanism-level stay-longer control works a little. For an API agent, the code-side equivalent is a minimum effort per approach before S6 may fire.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models over-spend on easy problems: after the first correct solution, later solutions rarely add accuracy or diversity.
numbers: '2 plus 3': o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. In over 92% of correct cases the first solution round already had the correct answer. Self-training that cut redundant rounds reduced tokens 48.6% on MATH500 with QwQ-32B-Preview at the same accuracy.
quote: o1-like models consumed 1,953% more tokens than conventional models
limits: Only open o1-like models; metrics rely on splitting solutions by marker words such as 'Alternatively'.
agent_relevance: Evidence for a stop rule (the monitor must also say 'enough'); supports G11 and G12. A cheap check after the first answer decides continuation.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: On controlled puzzles, reasoning models show three regimes: plain models better when easy, thinking models better at medium, both collapse at high. On easy puzzles the right answer comes early and the model keeps exploring wrong ones. On hard ones it fixates on an early wrong answer.
numbers: Puzzles such as Tower of Hanoi, varying disk count; models include Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking and DeepSeek-R1. Reasoning token use rises with complexity then falls near the collapse point, even with budget left.
limits: Disputed: later comments argued the collapse partly reflects output-token limits and unsolvable instances (from memory, not opened). Treat the regime pattern as likely, the collapse point as uncertain.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema: allocate by difficulty (G12), cap thinking (G11). Fixation on an early wrong path is the monitoring failure S6 should catch from outside.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification
finding: A linear probe on hidden states at intermediate answers predicts if that answer is correct. The model encodes correctness but does not use it to stop.
numbers: Probes reach ROC-AUC above 0.7 in distribution with expected calibration error below 0.1. Using the probe to exit early cut inference tokens 24% with no accuracy loss.
quote: reasoning models do encode a notion of correctness yet fail to exploit it
limits: Needs hidden-state access; trained per model; out-of-distribution results are lower than in-distribution.
agent_relevance: An internal monitoring signal exists but is not in the text. For an API agent, a sampled-agreement proxy is the closest, and only a hint (G4).

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in Large Language Models
finding: The same injected error is fixed when the user wrote it, but missed when the model's own turn contains it. A blind spot to own errors.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models: average blind spot 64.5%; 62.8% in non-maths domains; Claude Haiku 52.5% and Sonnet 4 41.4% in Table 7. Fine-tuning with 5,306 correction traces cut it 76.0%. Appending 'Wait' cut it 89.3%.
quote: Appending 'Wait' requires no training yet reduces the blind spot by 89.3%
limits: Injected, not natural, errors in the main test; 'Wait' effect measured on the blind-spot gap, not final accuracy.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct test of a Schoenfeld-style monitoring gap in models. Practical lever: present earlier output as a third party's work, or insert a cue like 'Wait', at S5/S8 only on a signal (G1).

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing: cut thinking at a cap, or append 'Wait' when the model tries to stop. 'Wait' makes it re-check and often fix errors.
numbers: s1-32B on AIME24: 50% without forcing to 57% with extra 'Wait' budget. Trained on 1,000 curated examples (s1K).
limits: Gain saturates and then falls if forced too long; the model is trained for this; one benchmark family.
agent_relevance: Scheduled doubt helps some tasks yet conflicts with G1 on easy ones. Reserve a forced 'Wait' for S6/S8 after a signal.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Search with evaluation and backtracking gives the model a place to abandon a line and resume elsewhere. It is an explicit control layer on top of the model.
numbers: Game of 24 with GPT-4: CoT solved 4% of tasks; ToT with breadth 5 solved 74%; breadth 1 solved 45%. GPT-4 generation with GPT-3.5 evaluation reached 64%.
limits: Costly in calls; evaluation by the same model; helps most where partial states can be judged.
agent_relevance: Prototype for the S6 operator tree. The 64% vs 74% line shows state-evaluation quality drives it, in line with G5.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Step-level error finding in maths: 3,400 cases with human-marked first error. Open process reward models fail to generalise to hard problems and lose to prompted critics.
numbers: Overall in Fig 1: o1-mini 87.9, GPT-4o-0806 61.9. QwQ-32B-Preview competitive with GPT-4o. Skywork-PRM-7B scored 70.8 on GSM8K and 53.6 on MATH, far lower on Olympiad-level.
limits: Competition-level problems; critics prompted per step; the best monitor is a reasoning model, which is costly.
agent_relevance: Quantifies the monitoring gap in maths: a strong reasoning critic can locate errors, small PRMs cannot on hard items. Pick the monitor model by difficulty.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false; they can estimate P(True) of their own answers and P(IK) that they know the answer. P(IK) transfers across tasks but is poorly calibrated on new tasks.
numbers: Reported by AUROC and calibration curves; larger models do better; self-evaluation improves when several own samples are shown first. No single headline percentage taken here.
limits: Mostly multiple choice, 2022 base models, not long maths proofs; RLHF models are miscalibrated until temperature is tuned.
agent_relevance: Older evidence that a confidence signal is usable; SCHEMA 4b says do not stop on verbal confidence, so use it only as a hint.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Large Language Models Have Intrinsic Meta-Cognition, but Need a Good Lens
finding: AutoMeco benchmarks 'lenses' (perplexity, entropy and so on) for step-level awareness of error, in the sense of feeling of error. MIRA, a training-free adjustment, improves the lenses.
numbers: Three maths datasets, three LLMs; AutoMeco validated against Best-of-N verification. Exact numbers not copied in this pass (abstract-level read).
limits: Needs logits.
agent_relevance: A menu of cheap token-level monitors; test each against verification before trusting it in S6.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Running code and giving the output back as feedback lets the model fix itself; explaining code in words helps without tests.
numbers: Gains up to 12% with unit tests on TransCoder and MBPP; 2 to 3% from explanation alone; 9% on the hardest Spider level.
limits: Code domain; strong gain needs execution feedback.
agent_relevance: Confirms that revision driven by real output (G2) works while self-opinion does not.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
finding: Verify output with tools (search, interpreter), then revise. The paper concludes external feedback is crucial.
numbers: Gains on QA, maths program synthesis and toxicity; per-task numbers not copied.
quote: crucial importance of external feedback in promoting the ongoing self-improvement of LLMs
limits: Per-task numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Same direction as c03, c04, c08.

source: Wang and Zhao (2024) Metacognitive Prompting Improves Understanding in Large Language Models
finding: Prompt that walks the model through understanding, judging, evaluating and confidence stages. Improves natural-language understanding tasks over chain of thought.
numbers: Five LLMs, language-understanding datasets (legal, medical entailment). Not maths. Gains reported per dataset, not copied.
limits: Not a maths or control study; the stage list is a human template with no stuck signal.
agent_relevance: Low value for S6. The same cost-benefit rule (G7) applies; not shown to beat token-matched plain prompting.
